title: Psalms
intro: 46 days through the Psalms, the Bible's book of prayers and songs, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Starting today, 46 days through the Psalms, the Bible's book of prayers and songs. Its 150 poems were written and collected over centuries and arranged into five books, which Jewish tradition compares to the five books of Moses. Psalm 1 opens the collection like a gateway: a person who delights in God's teaching (torah in Hebrew) is pictured as a deep-rooted, well-watered tree.

Psalm 3 is the first with a heading: "A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom," linking it to the revolt told in 2 Samuel 15. Headings like this are ancient, though many scholars think they were added after the psalms were written. "Lifts my head" pictures restored honor; in 2 Samuel, David leaves Jerusalem weeping, with his head covered.

A psalm for a clear night. Looking up at the moon and stars, the poet is amazed that the Maker of all that would pay attention to human beings at all. "Son of man" here is a Hebrew way of saying "a human being." The New Testament letter to the Hebrews quotes these lines and reads them in light of Jesus.

posts.display: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?
posts.caption: A lament: a prayer of complaint, often counted as the most common type of psalm. Four times in two verses the poet asks "How long?" Yet in just six verses the psalm moves from protest to trust and even song. The Psalms make room for grief, and even anger at God, inside prayer, something many first-time readers don't expect.

posts.display: The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.
posts.caption: Hebrew poetry doesn't rhyme sounds; it rhymes ideas. This is called parallelism: a second line echoes or extends the first in new words (heavens and skies, declare and proclaim). Psalm 19 moves from the wordless speech of the sky to the words of God's law. C.S. Lewis called it "the greatest poem in the Psalter."

posts.display: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning?
posts.caption: These are the words Jesus cries from the cross in Mark and Matthew. The heading names a tune, "The Doe of the Dawn," one of several melodies mentioned in the Psalms whose music is lost. The psalm moves from abandonment to praise. Christians have long read it as foreshadowing the crucifixion; Jewish tradition reads it differently, for example as a prayer of Queen Esther.

posts.display: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name.
posts.caption: When LORD is printed in capitals, it marks God's personal name in Hebrew, YHWH. Out of reverence, Jewish readers don't pronounce it and say Adonai ("my Lord") instead, and most English Bibles follow that custom. David, the psalm's traditional author, was a shepherd before he became king. Psalm 23 is often read at funerals by Jews and Christians alike.

posts.display: The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life— whom shall I dread?
posts.caption: A psalm of trust that also pleads with God not to turn away. Many Jewish communities recite it daily in the weeks leading up to and through the High Holy Days, a time of reflection and repentance. Its Latin opening, Dominus illuminatio mea ("The Lord is my light"), is the motto of the University of Oxford.

A psalm of thanksgiving from someone rescued from the edge of death ("You pulled me up from Sheol," the realm of the dead). The Hebrew verb for "stay the night" is used of a traveler lodging overnight: weeping arrives like an evening guest, but joy comes with the morning. In many communities Psalm 30 is part of the daily Jewish morning service.

In Luke's Gospel, Jesus' last words on the cross echo this line: "Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit." It was a prayer of trust long before that, and both traditions use it at night. Christians pray it at Compline, the last prayer before sleep, and the Jewish hymn Adon Olam ends with an echo of it: "Into His hand I entrust my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake."

Psalm 34 is an acrostic, a poem whose lines begin with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Its heading recalls David pretending to be insane to escape a Philistine king. 1 Samuel 21 names that king Achish, so the heading's "Abimelech" may be a title for Philistine kings. The poem turns that narrow escape into praise, and into this promise for people crushed by grief.

posts.display: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm.
posts.caption: "I waited patiently" translates a doubled Hebrew verb, literally "waiting, I waited," a way of adding emphasis. This is a thanksgiving for rescue from "the miry clay," a picture of sinking in a muddy pit. The Irish band U2 set this psalm to music as their song "40," which often closed their concerts.

posts.display: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?
posts.caption: Book Two of the Psalms begins here. The heading credits the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served as temple singers. The poet is far from Jerusalem, longing to worship there again, and a refrain repeats: "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" Psalm 43 shares that refrain, so many scholars think the two were once a single poem.

Roaring seas, quaking mountains and warring nations fill this psalm, and then God speaks. "Be still" translates a Hebrew word meaning "let go" or "stop," probably addressed first to the warring nations. "Selah," which appears 71 times in the Psalms, may be a musical cue such as a pause; its exact meaning is lost. Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" is based on Psalm 46.

The heading sets this psalm after the prophet Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12). "Create" is the Hebrew bara, the verb of Genesis 1, which the Bible uses only for God's creating. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles often number most psalms one lower, following the ancient Greek translation, so this is Psalm 50 there, known by its Latin first word, Miserere.

A lament over betrayal. A few verses later the poet reveals the worst of it: the enemy is not a stranger but "my companion and close friend," someone he once walked with to the house of God. This longing to escape inspired Felix Mendelssohn's anthem "Hear My Prayer," with its famous solo "O for the Wings of a Dove."

The heading sets this psalm in Gath, the Philistine city where David was seized (probably the same episode as Psalm 34), and names a tune, "A Dove on Distant Oaks." The verse holds a Hebrew wordplay: "my wanderings" (nodi) sounds like "bottle" (nod). The image is of God keeping every tear in a flask and writing it in a book, so that none is forgotten.

posts.display: In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.
posts.caption: In Hebrew, the first line says the poet's soul is "silence" toward God: a quiet, waiting trust. The heading mentions Jeduthun, one of the musicians appointed to lead worship in David's time (1 Chronicles 16). Around this calm swirl enemies who flatter and lie, and later verses repeat these lines as a refrain.

Psalm 68 is a victory hymn, and many scholars call its Hebrew among the hardest in the Psalms to translate. Amid marching armies and a thundering God, this passage stands out: the God of Sinai is defined by care for orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners. Protecting the fatherless and the widow is a constant theme of the Hebrew Bible's laws and prophets.

One of the few psalms in the voice of an old person. The speaker looks back on trusting God "from my youth" and asks not to be abandoned now that strength is failing, but to live long enough to pass the story on. Its opening lines closely match the start of Psalm 31, one sign that psalms drew on shared words of prayer.

Psalm 72, headed "Of Solomon," is a royal psalm: a prayer that the king will defend the poor and bring justice. Book Two closes here with a doxology, a short burst of praise, plus this editor's note. More psalms of David appear later, so many scholars think the note once ended an earlier collection of his prayers.

Book Three opens with the first of eleven psalms in a row credited to Asaph, one of David's chief musicians. It's a wisdom psalm: the poet nearly gave up after seeing the wicked prosper, until he entered God's sanctuary. "Portion" recalls the priests, who received no land because, as Numbers 18 says, God himself was their portion.

A pilgrim's song from the sons of Korah, longing for the temple courts. A doorkeeper held a humble post at the threshold, and 1 Chronicles names Korah's descendants among the temple gatekeepers, which makes the line especially fitting. The psalm's opening, "How lovely is Your dwelling place," became a movement of Brahms' German Requiem.

"Loving devotion" is this translation's term for the Hebrew hesed: loyal, committed, covenant love. The word appears more often in the Psalms than in any other book of the Bible. Here four great words meet like friends: hesed and faithfulness, righteousness and peace (shalom). The psalm prays for God to restore the land after a time of trouble.

Psalm 88 is often called the darkest psalm. Unlike almost every other lament, it never turns to hope or praise, and in Hebrew its very last word is "darkness." The heading credits Heman the Ezrahite. Many readers find it meaningful that a prayer this bleak was kept in the Bible: despair spoken to God is still treated as prayer.

Psalm 89 opens by celebrating God's promise that David's family would rule forever, then ends in shock: the king is defeated and his crown lies in the dust. Many scholars connect it with the fall of Jerusalem's royal line to Babylon. Book Three closes with this question unanswered, and Book Four opens with a prayer of Moses, from a time before Israel had kings.

The only psalm credited to Moses, "the man of God." It sets a human lifespan of seventy or eighty years against a God for whom a thousand years are like a single day. To "number our days" is to count them, aware that they are limited. Isaac Watts' hymn "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" is a paraphrase of this psalm.

Four names for God appear in these two verses: Most High (Elyon), Almighty (Shaddai), LORD (YHWH) and God (Elohim). Psalm 91 is a song of protection, traditionally prayed at night in both Christian Compline and Jewish bedtime prayers. In Matthew and Luke, the devil quotes it to Jesus during his temptation in the wilderness.

posts.display: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High, to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre.
posts.caption: This is the only psalm whose Hebrew heading names a day: "A song for the Sabbath day." According to the Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, the Levites sang a set psalm for each day of the week in the Jerusalem temple, and this one on the Sabbath. It remains part of Jewish Sabbath prayers.

Christians know Psalm 95 as the Venite, from its first word in Latin ("O come"), and for centuries it has opened daily morning prayer in many churches. In many synagogues it opens Kabbalat Shabbat, the Friday evening service that welcomes the Sabbath. It reads like an invitation sung by worshipers approaching the temple.

Psalm 100 is headed "A Psalm of thanksgiving," and it may have been sung as worshipers entered the temple gates. In English it's famous as the "Old Hundredth": a 16th-century metrical version, "All People That on Earth Do Dwell," whose tune is still sung worldwide, including for the doxology "Praise God, from Whom All Blessings Flow."

Psalm 103 begins and ends with "Bless the LORD, O my soul," and Psalm 104 opens the same way, so many scholars read them as a pair. Here forgiveness is pictured as infinite distance: east and west never meet. A few verses earlier, the psalm echoes God's description of himself to Moses in Exodus 34: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger."

Psalm 104 is a hymn to God as Creator, moving through sky, springs, mountains, animals and sea. Leviathan is a sea monster that ancient Near Eastern myths, and biblical poems like Isaiah 27, use as a symbol of chaos. Here it is simply one of God's creatures, made to play in the sea. Many scholars note parallels between this psalm and an Egyptian hymn to the sun-disk, the Aten.

Book Five opens with thanks from four groups God rescued: desert wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors caught in a storm. Each section repeats the same two refrains. For ancient Israel the sea was a symbol of chaos that only God could control, and many readers hear an echo of this passage in the Gospel stories of Jesus calming the storm.

posts.display: The LORD said to my Lord: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”
posts.caption: Notice LORD and Lord: God (YHWH) speaks to "my lord," the king. Many scholars think this royal psalm was first used when a king was crowned in Jerusalem. Jesus raises this verse in Mark 12, and it is often said to be the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New, where it is read as pointing to him. Jewish interpreters have read it about David or Abraham.

The shortest psalm, just two verses, and the shortest chapter in the Bible. It calls every nation to praise Israel's God. "Hallelujah" is Hebrew for "Praise Yah," a short form of God's name. Psalm 117 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118), a set of praise psalms sung at Jewish festivals.

The last psalm of the Hallel, sung at Passover. Mark says Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Last Supper, which many scholars think was this set of psalms. Jesus quotes the line about the rejected stone in Mark 12, and early Christians saw it as a picture of his rejection and vindication. "This is the day the LORD has made" became a beloved line of worship.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in praise of God's word. It's an acrostic in 22 stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and all eight lines of each stanza begin with that letter. This verse opens the stanza for the letter nun, and the Hebrew word for lamp, ner, begins with it.

posts.display: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.
posts.caption: Psalms 120 to 134 are each headed "A song of ascents." Many scholars think pilgrims sang them while going up to Jerusalem, a city in the hills, for the great festivals. The question-and-answer opening may have been sung by two voices. Psalm 121 has long been a traveler's prayer, often said before journeys.

Psalm 130 begins "Out of the depths I cry to You," known by its Latin opening, De profundis. It is one of the seven Penitential Psalms of Christian tradition, and has long been prayed for the dead. Here waiting for God is compared to night watchmen on a city wall longing for dawn, and the line is repeated, as if the night were long.

posts.display: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!
posts.caption: Another song of ascents, perhaps sung when pilgrims from many towns gathered in Jerusalem. The psalm compares unity to fragrant anointing oil running down the beard of Aaron, the first high priest, and to the dew of Mount Hermon. Its opening words in Hebrew, Hinei ma tov, begin a much-loved Jewish song.

A lament from the exile, after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem around 586 BC and deported many of its people. The next verse asks: "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" The psalm ends with a shocking curse on Babylon's children, the raw anger of people who had seen their city destroyed. Its opening became the reggae song "Rivers of Babylon."

Psalm 139 is a meditation on being completely known: God knows the poet's thoughts, path and words before they are spoken, and there is nowhere to escape God's presence. Here the poet pictures God weaving a body together before birth. The psalm ends with an invitation: "Search me, O God, and know my heart."

Psalm 145 is the only psalm headed "A Psalm of praise" (tehillah), and the plural of that word, Tehillim, is the Hebrew name of the whole book. It is an acrostic, and observant Jews recite it, within a prayer called Ashrei, three times a day. The Talmud says whoever does so is assured a share in the world to come.

Psalms 146 to 150 close the book, and each begins and ends with "Hallelujah." This pairing is striking: the God who counts the stars and calls each by name also binds up individual wounds. The psalm speaks of God gathering Israel's exiles and rebuilding Jerusalem, so many scholars date it after the return from Babylon.

The last verse of the Psalms. Psalm 150 calls for praise with horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing and cymbals, then includes every living, breathing thing. The book has traveled from Psalm 1's quiet blessing through grief, anger and thanks to this final "Hallelujah." Jews, and later Christians, have prayed these poems for over two thousand years. Thank you for reading them with me.
